candidates.attacker_control: The URL string is fully attacker-chosen by any party able to influence the job's build-step configuration (Job/Configure), by JCasC, or by a pipeline invocation that passes a build parameter/env value into the `testPlanUrl` argument of `zohoQEngineTestPlanExecution(...)`; none of these values is validated beyond the `https://` prefix and segment count. The host component (resourceSplit[0]) and the portal segment (resourceSplit[1]) are otherwise unvalidated; projectID/testPlanID are only checked with extractLongValue() but the checked local variables are discarded and the original (possibly `+`- or zero-prefixed) strings are used in the URL path.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked and accounted for: (a) the plugin enforces `https://` and requires exactly 6 path segments, so malformed or multi-slash URLs are rejected and no attacker-chosen string with a slash can be smuggled into a segment; (b) `extractLongValue` rejects non-numeric/<=0 project and test-plan IDs; (c) Java's HttpClient (ProxyConfiguration.newHttpClient()) does not follow redirects by default, so the key is not leaked via redirect to a third host; (d) the API key and the URL are normally supplied by the same configurer, which reduces the privilege boundary (a Job/Configure holder can replace the key anyway) — this is the main argument against treating it as a vulnerability rather than hardening, so the finding is submitted as a lead with medium confidence; (e) no test code, no Jelly config, and no documentation exist in the snapshot that would constrain the URL to a Zoho domain or demonstrate a lower-privileged input path to testPlanUrl.
candidates.impact: Two concrete effects from the controller JVM: (1) SSRF — the Jenkins controller issues HTTPS PATCH/GET requests (with attacker-shaped path and JSON body) to any host/port reachable from the controller, including internal-only services, with the response body parsed and partially echoed to the build log; (2) credential exposure — the stored QEngine API key is transmitted as a bearer token to the unvalidated destination, so anyone who can point the step's URL at a server they control receives the secret in cleartext (subject to the prerequisites), and a single mis-typed/malicious URL silently leaks the key with no allowlist or host check to prevent it. The plugin's own form validation has the same 6-segment-only check (lines 63-75), so the misconfiguration is never surfaced.
candidates.prerequisites: Attacker can set or influence the build step's testPlanUrl for a job that has a stored QEngine API key (or can induce such a build). The Jenkins controller must be able to reach the attacker-controlled/internal HTTPS endpoint. No permission check, host allowlist, or redirect check exists in the plugin to stop this.
candidates.root_cause: QEnginePluginBuilder.perform() derives the API base URL by splitting the configured testPlanUrl on "//" and "/" and accepts any value where the string starts with "https://" and the post-authority portion contains exactly 6 slash-separated segments; the host/port is never constrained (no Zoho domain allowlist, no URI re-parsing/authority comparison). The derived authority and path segments are concatenated into request URLs in CommonUtils.executeTestPlan()/getTestPlanStatus(), where the job's API key is attached verbatim: `httpRequest.setHeader(AUTHORIZATION, API_TOKEN + apiKey.getPlainText().trim())`, i.e. `Authorization: Bearer <plaintext secret>` is sent to whatever host the configuration string designates, and the controller (not an agent) makes the request via ProxyConfiguration.newHttpClient().
candidates.title: Stored API key is forwarded to an arbitrary, unvalidated HTTPS host derived from the job-configured testPlanUrl (SSRF / credential exfiltration)
candidates.trace: perform() (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:108-140) reads testPlanUrl -> startsWith("https://") (line 111) -> split("//") (line 114) -> split("/") with resourceSplit.length==6 (lines 115-122) -> requestUrl = protocolSplit[0]+"//"+resourceSplit[0] (line 118) -> CommonUtils.executeTestPlan(apiKey, requestUrl, portalName, projectID, testPlanID, ...) (line 156) -> executeUrl = requestUrl + "/api/v1/integration/" + portalName + "/projects/" + projectID + "/testplans/" + testPlanID + "/execute" (CommonUtils.java:52-53) -> `new URI(executeUrl)` + setHeader("Authorization", "Bearer " + apiKey.getPlainText().trim()) (lines 57-59) -> httpClient.send(PATCH) (line 74). The same pattern repeats for the polling GET in getTestPlanStatus() (CommonUtils.java:114-138). The server's JSON response fields (`message`, `scheduleexecution.status`) are then printed into the build console and used to set the build result (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:159-168), so the response is partially observable to the log reader.
candidates.unverified: Not verified at runtime: whether real deployments expose testPlanUrl to lower-privileged actors (build parameters/pipeline `params.`), and whether the Jenkins threat model for this instance treats Job/Configure as trusted for the job's stored secret. The absence of a host allowlist and of any permission check is verified by source text; the concrete exfiltration scenario depends on deployment configuration not present in the snapshot.
candidates.weakness_type: SSRF with sensitive credential disclosure (CWE-918; CWE-522/CWE-441 pattern)

coverage_summary: Source scope reports 14 model-visible files, 0 excluded/oversized/symlinked files, with the same filters applied to B0 and P1. I read both Java files in full (CommonUtils.java 262 lines; QEnginePluginBuilder.java 229 lines), pom.xml, README.md, both GitHub workflows, .mvn/extensions.xml, .github/dependabot.yml, and all four help-*.html resources; .gitignore and LICENSE.md were not read (no security relevance). The P1 relation scope reports 14/14 files indexed, 2 Java files parsed with 0 parse errors, 33 symbols, 127 calls / 37 edges / 3 facts, but with data-flow and control-flow "not_implemented", semantic resolution "not_implemented", 121 unresolved calls, Spring/annotation handling unverified and no test facts — so the index was used only for navigation and every index candidate (the call edges perform->executeTestPlan/getTestPlanStatus/extractLongValue, the constructor's Secret.fromString call site) was re-verified against source text. No builds, tests, or scanners were executed, and no runtime/reachability behavior is claimed.
limitations: Only two Java source files exist; the review is limited to their source-level behavior. No tests, no Jelly/UI configuration in the snapshot, so form binding and rendering behavior (e.g. how the Secret field is displayed/round-tripped) could not be verified from source.

The relation index provides syntax-only call/containment candidates with no data flow, control flow, or semantic resolution (121 unresolved calls), so data-flow paths into the HTTP sinks were established by manual reading, not by the index.

Whether testPlanUrl can be supplied by a lower-privileged actor (build parameter, pipeline env/params, JCasC) is a deployment choice outside the snapshot; the selected candidate's impact therefore depends on configuration not visible here.

External semantics of the QEngine API (statuses such as failed/aborted, the meaning of HTTP 202, expected URL format) are not documented in the repository, so the fail-open status handling could not be resolved.
No runtime confirmation, exploitation, or scanner run was performed; all findings remain source-level leads.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing permission checks on the four @POST form-validation methods (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:61-97; doCheckTestPlanUrl even carries @SuppressWarnings("lgtm[jenkins/no-permission-check]"), and repo-wide search finds no checkPermission/Jenkins.get().checkPermission call).
rejected_leads.reason: Explicit anti-pattern with a real tell, but no demonstrable impact: these methods only inspect the submitted string and return constant FormValidation messages; they perform no network I/O, read no files/secrets, and leak nothing, so per the review standard this is a hardening gap rather than an evidence-backed vulnerability. @POST (org.kohsuke.stapler.verb.POST) is present, so the CSRF angle is also covered.

rejected_leads.lead: Integer overflow in `long pollingInterval = (maxWaitTime * 60) / (pollCount - 1) * 1000;` (CommonUtils.java:124) can produce a huge positive interval (e.g. maxWaitTime=1e9 overflows to ~1,974,202,368 ms ≈ 22.8 days of Thread.sleep at line 195), plus doCheckMaxWaitTime only requires maxWaitTime > 0 and perform only replaces negative values with 180 (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:86-90, 146-148).
rejected_leads.reason: Real arithmetic bug, but the value is job-config-supplied: a configurer who can set it can already occupy an executor with an ordinary build step, so the incremental attacker capability/impact is weak. Also several overflow outcomes are negative and simply raise IllegalArgumentException (caught -> FAILURE).

rejected_leads.lead: getTestPlanStatus() returns true (build SUCCESS) in the `default` branch for any unrecognized scheduleexecution status (CommonUtils.java:184-189), so a failed-but-unrecognized test-plan state can be reported as a passing gate.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible integrity weakness in the gate, but it is an explicit developer choice, the set of real QEngine statuses is not derivable from the snapshot (no docs/tests), and the status originates from the configured server rather than from a clearly lower-privileged attacker. Too uncertain to prefer over the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Unvalidated buildName is printed to the build console and appended to the JSON body (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:150-154, CommonUtils.java:66-73), allowing log-line/ANSI injection via newlines/escape sequences.
rejected_leads.reason: Low impact and requires configuration input; JSON body construction is properly escaped by JSONObject. Not a credential or trust-boundary issue.

rejected_leads.lead: CommonUtils.readContents() allocates a fixed 500 KB char buffer and is dead code in this snapshot.
rejected_leads.reason: No caller exists, fixed-size buffer (not unbounded), and no security-relevant behavior; no finding.

rejected_leads.lead: CI/CD workflow supply chain (.github/workflows/cd.yaml, jenkins-security-scan.yml use reusable workflows pinned to moving tags @v1/@v2 rather than commit SHAs).
rejected_leads.reason: Standard Jenkins plugin templates; no untrusted checkout/execution of fork code (no pull_request_target with secrets exposure), and this is a repository-hardening observation rather than a source vulnerability in the shipped plugin.

summary: Reviewed the complete Zoho QEngine Jenkins plugin snapshot (14 files; 2 Java files, both read end-to-end). The build step accepts a user-supplied "test plan URL" from job configuration, validates it only by an `https://` prefix test and a hard-coded segment count, then concatenates the derived authority/path into API URLs and sends the stored QEngine API key as an `Authorization: Bearer <plaintext>` header from the Jenkins controller JVM. I found no host allowlist and no permission checks anywhere in the code (search for `checkPermission`/`RequirePOST` returns zero hits). The strongest evidence-backed lead is the unconstrained-host credential/SSRF path (CWE-918/CWE-522 pattern); other candidate leads (missing permission checks on the `@POST` form-validation methods, an int-overflow that can produce a ~23-day `Thread.sleep`, and a fail-open `default` branch in the status switch) were rejected as unsupported or lower-impact and are listed below. No runtime testing was performed; all statements are source-level.
